conditions.name: Pattern consistent with an acute stress response
conditions.summary: A short-term rise in physiological and emotional arousal in response to a specific demand, such as an anomaly, a critical task or a disagreement. It usually fades once the situation is resolved.

indicator_rules.note: Heart rate above personal baseline may reflect sympathetic arousal (MedlinePlus Stress); no validated absolute threshold; baseline-relative design value.
RMSSD more than 20% below baseline; stress is associated with reduced parasympathetic (vagal) HRV (Kim 2018 meta-analysis); no validated absolute threshold; baseline-relative design value.
Breathing rate above baseline consistent with arousal (NIMH GAD: feeling out of breath); no validated absolute threshold; baseline-relative design value.
Facial muscle tension above baseline; NIMH lists muscle tension among anxiety/stress symptoms; no validated absolute threshold; baseline-relative design value.
Composite stress index above personal baseline; no validated absolute threshold; baseline-relative design value.
GAD-2 item (0-3); GAD-2 total >=3 is the preferred cut-point (Kroenke 2007: sensitivity 86%, specificity 83% for GAD).
GAD-2 item (0-3); GAD-2 total >=3 is the preferred cut-point (Kroenke 2007: sensitivity 86%, specificity 83% for GAD).
High perceived workload is a named contributor in the NASA sleep/work-overload risk; acute stress follows an external demand (NIMH).
Feeling angry or easily upset is a listed stress symptom (MedlinePlus Stress).
Stress degrades cognitive and motor performance (local CNS file; NIMH).
Loss of sleep is a common stress symptom (NIMH stress fact sheet).

probable_causes: Interpersonal disagreement or conflict with crew or ground
conditions.isolation_relevance: In a small isolated habitat there are few ways to step away from a stressor, and acute stress can degrade performance on safety-critical tasks. NASA lists isolation and confinement as drivers of cognitive and behavioral decrements, and stress degrades cognitive and psychomotor performance.
conditions.orientative_interpretation: Your signals may indicate a short-term stress response: heart and breathing activity are above your usual baseline and you reported feeling tense or overloaded. This is a normal reaction to demand and often settles with a brief recovery break. A few minutes of slow breathing and a short pause may help.
conditions.escalation_criteria: If the safety item is answered yes at any time, the app's safety protocol takes priority over this orientation. Discuss with your flight surgeon or behavioral health team if stress symptoms persist for 2 weeks or more, interfere with daily tasks, or if you feel unable to cope (MedlinePlus Stress). Repeated sessions with this pattern across several days should also be reviewed.
red_flags: Increasing use of substances or sleep aids to manage stress
Chest pain, fainting or severe shortness of breath (needs medical evaluation)
conditions.camera_limits: Heart rate, HRV, breathing rate and facial tension can also change with exercise, caffeine, talking, posture, temperature or illness; none of them alone can distinguish stress from physical exertion. Expression classifiers cannot read emotions reliably on their own.

conditions.name: Pattern consistent with elevated anxiety
conditions.summary: Persistent nervousness or worry that is hard to control, often with muscle tension, restlessness, poor sleep and difficulty concentrating, and that can continue without an immediate threat.

indicator_rules.note: Heart rate above personal baseline may reflect sympathetic arousal (MedlinePlus Stress); no validated absolute threshold; baseline-relative design value.
RMSSD more than 15% below baseline; stress is associated with reduced parasympathetic (vagal) HRV (Kim 2018 meta-analysis); no validated absolute threshold; baseline-relative design value.
Breathing rate above baseline consistent with arousal (NIMH GAD: feeling out of breath); no validated absolute threshold; baseline-relative design value.
Facial muscle tension above baseline; NIMH lists muscle tension among anxiety/stress symptoms; no validated absolute threshold; baseline-relative design value.
More fear-classified expressions than baseline; classifier output only; no validated absolute threshold; baseline-relative design value.
Head stability more than 10% below baseline may reflect restlessness; no validated absolute threshold; baseline-relative design value.
GAD-2 item (0-3); GAD-2 total >=3 is the preferred cut-point (Kroenke 2007: sensitivity 86%, specificity 83% for GAD).
GAD-2 item (0-3); GAD-2 total >=3 is the preferred cut-point (Kroenke 2007: sensitivity 86%, specificity 83% for GAD).
Trouble falling or staying asleep is a listed GAD symptom (NIMH).
Hard time concentrating is a listed GAD symptom (NIMH).
Irritability / feeling on edge is a listed GAD symptom (NIMH).
Headaches and muscle aches are listed GAD symptoms (NIMH).

probable_causes: Ongoing uncertainty about mission events or family on Earth
High workload and perceived lack of control
Personal or family history of anxiety
conditions.isolation_relevance: The NASA evidence report found anxiety to be the most frequently reported behavioral symptom in Shuttle crews (24 instances over 28.84 person-years). Anxiety has also been documented in Antarctic personnel, and in isolation there are fewer outlets and less access to in-person support.
conditions.orientative_interpretation: Your answers suggest that nervousness or hard-to-control worry has been frequent recently, and your physiological signals may indicate elevated arousal. This pattern may indicate anxiety worth addressing early. Slow breathing, a scheduled worry window and talking with someone you trust may help, and this is worth discussing with your flight surgeon or behavioral health team.
conditions.escalation_criteria: If the safety item is answered yes at any time, the app's safety protocol takes priority over this orientation. A GAD-2 total of 3 or more (q_nervous + q_worry) warrants further evaluation with the GAD-7 or a clinician (Kroenke 2007). Refer to the behavioral health team if symptoms persist on most days, cause avoidance, or interfere with work or sleep (NIMH).
red_flags: GAD-2 total of 3 or more on repeated sessions
conditions.camera_limits: No camera indicator (heart rate, HRV, breathing, facial tension, fear-classified expressions, head movement) can identify anxiety on its own; each also changes with exertion, caffeine, temperature, speech or illness. Questionnaire support (GAD-2) is required before this pattern can be ranked highly.

conditions.name: Pattern consistent with a panic-like surge of arousal
conditions.summary: A sudden surge of intense fear with strong body symptoms such as pounding heart, fast breathing, sweating or trembling, which typically peaks within minutes.

indicator_rules.note: Heart rate above personal baseline may reflect a sudden arousal surge (MedlinePlus Stress); no validated absolute threshold; baseline-relative design value.
Breathing rate above baseline consistent with arousal (NIMH GAD: feeling out of breath); no validated absolute threshold; baseline-relative design value.
RMSSD more than 30% below baseline; stress is associated with reduced parasympathetic (vagal) HRV (Kim 2018 meta-analysis); no validated absolute threshold; baseline-relative design value.
Fear-classified expressions doubled vs baseline; classifier output only; no validated absolute threshold; baseline-relative design value.
Head stability more than 15% below baseline may reflect trembling or agitation; no validated absolute threshold; baseline-relative design value.
Feeling nervous, anxious or on edge nearly every day (GAD-2 item).
GAD-2 item (0-3); GAD-2 total >=3 is the preferred cut-point (Kroenke 2007: sensitivity 86%, specificity 83% for GAD).
GAD-2 item (0-3); GAD-2 total >=3 is the preferred cut-point (Kroenke 2007: sensitivity 86%, specificity 83% for GAD).
New stimulant or medication may mimic or trigger arousal symptoms; review with the flight surgeon.
Difficulty concentrating during high arousal.

probable_causes: Acute anxiety reaction to a threatening or uncertain event
Medical causes that can mimic panic (heart rhythm problems, low blood sugar)
conditions.isolation_relevance: Panic-like episodes in a confined vehicle can be frightening and affect task performance, and because attacks can be mistaken for a heart problem, medical causes must be ruled out with the flight surgeon. Communication delays on exploration missions make early recognition and self-management skills more important.
conditions.orientative_interpretation: Your signals show a strong rise in heart and breathing rate compared with your baseline, together with intense nervousness. This may indicate a panic-like surge of arousal. Such episodes usually peak within 10 to 20 minutes. Slowing your exhale and grounding your attention may help, and any chest pain or fainting should be checked medically right away.
conditions.escalation_criteria: If the safety item is answered yes at any time, the app's safety protocol takes priority over this orientation. Contact the flight surgeon immediately if there is chest pain, fainting, severe shortness of breath or symptoms that do not settle, because panic attacks can be mistaken for a heart attack (MedlinePlus). Involve the behavioral health team if episodes recur or interfere with work, relationships or self-confidence.
red_flags: Symptoms lasting more than an hour
conditions.camera_limits: A high heart rate and fast breathing on camera look the same after exercise, during fever, with stimulants or with heart rhythm problems. The camera cannot tell panic from a medical emergency, and rPPG heart rate is unreliable with movement. A questionnaire and clinical review are required.

conditions.name: Pattern consistent with low mood (depressive symptoms)
conditions.summary: Persistent low, sad or empty mood and/or loss of interest or pleasure, often with low energy, sleep and appetite changes and poor concentration.

indicator_rules.note: Reduced facial expressivity vs baseline; expression is culture- and person-dependent and cannot indicate mood alone; no validated absolute threshold; baseline-relative design value.
Fewer positive expressions than personal baseline; no validated absolute threshold; baseline-relative design value.
More sad-classified expressions than personal baseline; classifier output, not a mood measure; no validated absolute threshold; baseline-relative design value.
Composite wellbeing index more than 20% below baseline; no validated absolute threshold; baseline-relative design value.
PHQ-2 item (0-3); PHQ-2 total >=3 is the validated screening cut-point (Kroenke 2003: sensitivity 82.9%, specificity 90.0% for major depression).
PHQ-2 item (0-3); PHQ-2 total >=3 is the validated screening cut-point (Kroenke 2003: sensitivity 82.9%, specificity 90.0% for major depression).
Fatigue or lack of energy is a listed depression symptom (NIMH); PHQ-9 item.
Sleep difficulty is a listed depression symptom (NIMH).
Appetite change is a listed depression symptom (NIMH).
Difficulty concentrating is a listed depression symptom (NIMH).
Loneliness is linked to poorer mental health (Hawkley & Cacioppo 2010).

probable_causes: Prolonged isolation and separation from family
Medical causes (e.g. thyroid, anemia, medication effects) to be ruled out by the flight surgeon
conditions.isolation_relevance: Two of seven NASA Shuttle-Mir astronauts (29%) reported depressive symptoms, depression may have contributed to an early mission end in 1985 (Soyuz T14-Salyut 7), and one Mars-500 crew member developed depressive symptoms. In small crews, mood changes are often noticed only after they already affect performance.
conditions.orientative_interpretation: Your answers suggest low mood and/or reduced interest on many days recently, and your expressions appear less varied than your usual baseline. This pattern may indicate depressive symptoms and is worth discussing with your flight surgeon or behavioral health team. Scheduling small rewarding activities, keeping a regular sleep schedule and staying connected with people may help in the meantime.
conditions.escalation_criteria: If the safety item is answered yes at any time, the app's safety protocol takes priority over this orientation. A PHQ-2 total of 3 or more (q_mood_low + q_anhedonia) should be followed by the PHQ-9 or a clinician interview (Kroenke 2003); PHQ-9 scores of 10 or more indicate at least moderate symptoms (Kroenke 2001). Refer to the behavioral health team if symptoms are present most of the day, nearly every day, for 2 weeks or more (NIMH).
red_flags: Symptoms nearly every day for 2 weeks or more
Thoughts of death or self-harm (safety protocol)
conditions.camera_limits: Reduced expressivity, fewer smiles or more sad-classified frames cannot indicate depression on their own: they vary with fatigue, concentration, culture, personality, lighting and camera angle. Camera evidence alone is capped well below a high-ranking finding; PHQ-2 answers are required.

conditions.name: Pattern consistent with adjustment difficulty
conditions.summary: Emotional or behavioral strain (nervousness, sadness, tension, poor sleep) that begins after a major change or stressor, typically within the first months, and usually eases as the person adapts.

indicator_rules.note: Composite stress index above personal baseline; no validated absolute threshold; baseline-relative design value.
Heart rate above personal baseline may reflect sympathetic arousal (MedlinePlus Stress); no validated absolute threshold; baseline-relative design value.
Composite wellbeing index more than 15% below baseline; no validated absolute threshold; baseline-relative design value.
RMSSD more than 15% below baseline; stress is associated with reduced parasympathetic (vagal) HRV (Kim 2018 meta-analysis); no validated absolute threshold; baseline-relative design value.
Composite fatigue index above personal baseline; no validated absolute threshold; baseline-relative design value.
Adjustment symptoms usually begin within 3 months of a stressor (MedlinePlus); the first mission quarter is the main adaptation period.
Nervousness or tension is a listed adjustment-disorder symptom (MedlinePlus).
Sadness or hopelessness is a listed adjustment-disorder symptom (MedlinePlus).
Sleep disruption is common early in flight (local CNS file; Barger 2014).
Separation from family is a reported stressor in orbit (Kanas 2016; local CNS file).
High workload during the adaptation period.
Defiant or impulsive behavior and tension are listed symptoms (MedlinePlus).
Reduced concentration during adaptation.
Fatigue during early adaptation.

probable_causes: Transition into the mission environment (new routines, microgravity or confinement)
Separation from family and usual supports
conditions.isolation_relevance: Kanas (2016) reports that the most common psychiatric problems in space are adjustment reactions presenting with anxiety or depressive symptoms, which usually resolve as the person adapts. Most physiological functions adjust to microgravity within the first 3 to 14 days (local CNS file).
conditions.orientative_interpretation: Your answers and signals may indicate that you are still adjusting to the mission environment: some tension, lower mood or poorer sleep compared with your baseline. This is common in the early phase and usually eases with time, routine and support. Keeping regular sleep and meals, staying in contact with family and pacing your workload may help.
conditions.escalation_criteria: If the safety item is answered yes at any time, the app's safety protocol takes priority over this orientation. Discuss with the behavioral health team if symptoms are severe enough to affect work or social life, persist beyond the early mission phase, or if PHQ-2 or GAD-2 totals reach 3 or more (MedlinePlus; Kroenke 2003; Kroenke 2007).
red_flags: Symptoms that keep worsening rather than easing
conditions.camera_limits: Camera indices cannot tell whether a change is linked to a recent stressor; that context comes only from the user's answers and mission timeline. Physiological shifts early in flight may also reflect fluid shifts and space motion sickness rather than adjustment.

conditions.name: Pattern consistent with insomnia symptoms
conditions.summary: Difficulty falling asleep, staying asleep or waking too early despite a sleep opportunity, with daytime consequences such as sleepiness or poor concentration.

indicator_rules.note: Eyelid closure (PERCLOS) above personal baseline consistent with drowsiness; no validated absolute threshold; baseline-relative design value (absolute PERCLOS ranges are defined by agent B reference_ranges).
More yawning than personal baseline consistent with sleepiness; no validated absolute threshold; baseline-relative design value.
Composite fatigue index above personal baseline; no validated absolute threshold; baseline-relative design value.
Poor perceived sleep quality; dissatisfaction with sleep is a core ISI item (ISI, Morin).
Adults need at least 7 hours per day; less is short sleep (CDC).
Astronauts averaged about 6 h per night in flight (Barger 2014); 6 h for 14 days produced cumulative cognitive deficits (Van Dongen 2003).
KSS 7 = 'sleepy but no effort to keep awake' (anchor label; Akerstedt & Gillberg 1990); anchor-based, not a validated clinical cut-off.
Worry is linked to trouble falling or staying asleep (NIMH GAD).
Daytime functioning impairment is an ISI item.
New sleep aid, stimulant or medication may affect sleep; about 75% of ISS crew reported using sleep medication at some point (Barger 2014).

probable_causes: Noise, light, temperature and vibration in the sleep area
Carbon dioxide levels and space motion sickness (local CNS file)
conditions.isolation_relevance: Sleep deficiency is common in spaceflight: astronauts averaged 6.09 h per night on ISS and 5.96 h on Shuttle missions despite 8.5 h scheduled, and about three-quarters of ISS crew used sleep medication at some point (Barger 2014). Sleep loss is linked to performance errors, fatigue and mood and team problems (NASA OCHMO).
conditions.orientative_interpretation: Your answers suggest poorer or shorter sleep than recommended, and your eyes and face may show signs of daytime sleepiness. This may indicate an insomnia pattern. A fixed wake time, getting out of bed when you cannot sleep, and dimming light before sleep may help; if it continues, it is worth discussing with your flight surgeon.
conditions.escalation_criteria: If the safety item is answered yes at any time, the app's safety protocol takes priority over this orientation. Discuss with the flight surgeon if poor sleep continues for 2 weeks or more, if daytime sleepiness affects critical tasks, or before starting or changing any sleep medication. A full Insomnia Severity Index score of 15 or more falls in the clinical insomnia range (ISI scoring).
red_flags: Loud snoring or breathing pauses reported by crewmates
conditions.camera_limits: Eyelid closure, yawning and fatigue indices show sleepiness, not its cause; they cannot tell insomnia from simple sleep restriction, circadian misalignment or medication effects. Sleep history (questionnaire) is required.

conditions.name: Pattern consistent with circadian misalignment
conditions.summary: A mismatch between the body clock and the work/sleep schedule, so that the person tries to sleep or work at the wrong biological time, leading to shorter sleep, sleepiness and reduced performance.

indicator_rules.note: Session during the usual biological night (00:00-05:59 local); performance and sleep inertia are worst near the circadian low (Hilditch 2019). Time window is a design choice, no validated absolute threshold.

Eyelid closure (PERCLOS) above personal baseline consistent with drowsiness; no validated absolute threshold; baseline-relative design value (absolute PERCLOS ranges are defined by agent B reference_ranges).
More yawning than personal baseline consistent with sleepiness; no validated absolute threshold; baseline-relative design value.
Composite fatigue index above personal baseline; no validated absolute threshold; baseline-relative design value.
Head stability more than 10% below baseline may reflect head nodding; no validated absolute threshold; baseline-relative design value.
KSS 7 = 'sleepy but no effort to keep awake' (anchor label); KSS rises with time awake and varies strongly with time of day (Akerstedt & Gillberg 1990).
Short sleep (<7 h; CDC); misalignment shortens sleep (Flynn-Evans 2016).
Misalignment reduces sleep quality when sleep falls in the biological day (local CNS file).
Misalignment and long work hours are linked to attention deficits and errors (local CNS file).
Daytime fatigue.
Circadian disruption is linked to altered glucose regulation and metabolism (local CNS file).
Misalignment is associated with increased medication use (Flynn-Evans 2016).

probable_causes: Shifted or rotating schedules (slam shifts, docking or EVA preparation)
About 16 sunrises and sunsets per day in low Earth orbit
conditions.isolation_relevance: On long-duration ISS missions, circadian misalignment occurred on roughly 20% of flight days with about one hour of sleep lost per night (local CNS file, citing Flynn-Evans et al. 2016). In Mars-500, two of six crew drifted to non-24 h or split sleep-wake patterns and were asleep while others were awake for about 20% of the mission (Basner 2013).
conditions.orientative_interpretation: This session ran during the usual biological night and/or your answers and eye signals may indicate sleepiness and shortened sleep. This pattern may indicate that your body clock and schedule are out of step. Timed bright light at the start of your day, dim light before sleep and a consistent anchor sleep period may help.
conditions.escalation_criteria: Discuss with the flight surgeon and mission planners if misalignment is repeated over several days, before upcoming schedule shifts, if sleepiness affects safety-critical tasks, or if medication is being considered (NASA-STD-3001 V1 6001 circadian shifting and fatigue management).
conditions.camera_limits: Clock time and eye signals cannot reveal a person's internal circadian phase; a night-time session may be a planned shift. Drowsiness signs are shared with sleep deprivation and insomnia. Sleep timing from the questionnaire or schedule is needed.

conditions.name: Pattern consistent with sleep deprivation (acute or accumulated)
conditions.summary: Too little sleep over one or more nights, leading to sleepiness, slower reactions, lapses of attention and irritability. Deficits build up over consecutive short nights even when the person feels adapted.

indicator_rules.note: Eyelid closure (PERCLOS) above personal baseline consistent with drowsiness; no validated absolute threshold; baseline-relative design value (absolute PERCLOS ranges are defined by agent B reference_ranges).
More yawning than personal baseline consistent with sleepiness; no validated absolute threshold; baseline-relative design value.
Composite fatigue index above personal baseline; no validated absolute threshold; baseline-relative design value.
Head stability more than 10% below baseline may reflect head nodding; no validated absolute threshold; baseline-relative design value.
Six hours per night for 14 days produced cumulative cognitive deficits (Van Dongen 2003); in-flight averages were about 6 h (Barger 2014).
Less than 7 h per day is short sleep for adults (CDC).
KSS 7 = 'sleepy but no effort to keep awake' (anchor label; Akerstedt & Gillberg 1990).
Vigilant attention is the function most consistently affected by sleep loss (Lim & Dinges 2008).
Sleep loss is linked to mood and team problems (NASA OCHMO sleep brief).

probable_causes: Shortened sleep opportunity due to workload or schedule
conditions.isolation_relevance: Astronauts commonly experience sleep deprivation (NASA HRP sleep risk), averaging about 6 h per night in flight versus 8.5 h scheduled (Barger 2014). With chronic restriction, subjective sleepiness levels off while performance keeps declining, so people may underestimate their impairment (Van Dongen 2003).
conditions.orientative_interpretation: You reported short sleep and your eyes and face may show signs of sleepiness compared with your baseline. This may indicate accumulated sleep loss. Because chronic sleep loss can impair attention even when you feel used to it, it is worth protecting your next sleep period and, if possible, taking a short strategic nap before critical tasks.
conditions.escalation_criteria: Inform the flight surgeon and mission planning if sleep has been under 6 h for several consecutive nights, if KSS is 8-9 before critical tasks, or if microsleeps occur. Consider rescheduling safety-critical tasks (NASA-STD-3001 V1 4014 limits on workday and sleep periods).
red_flags: Reliance on stimulants to stay awake
conditions.camera_limits: PERCLOS, yawning and head nodding show drowsiness but cannot measure how much sleep was lost or why; illness, medication, boredom and low light can produce similar signals. Sleep hours must come from the user or a sleep tracker.

conditions.name: Pattern consistent with sleep inertia (grogginess after waking)
conditions.summary: A temporary period of grogginess and reduced performance right after waking, strongest in the first 30 minutes and worse after sleep loss or when waking during the biological night.

More yawning than personal baseline consistent with sleepiness; no validated absolute threshold; baseline-relative design value.
Composite fatigue index above personal baseline; no validated absolute threshold; baseline-relative design value.
Head stability more than 10% below baseline may reflect head nodding; no validated absolute threshold; baseline-relative design value.

Sleep inertia effects are greatest near the circadian low in core body temperature (Hilditch 2019); time window is a design choice, no validated absolute threshold. Ask whether the session is within 30 min of waking.
KSS 7 = 'sleepy but no effort to keep awake' (anchor label).
Prior sleep loss increases sleep inertia (Hilditch 2019).
Reduced alertness and performance after waking (Hilditch 2019).
Sleep aids may prolong grogginess; review with the flight surgeon.
Disturbed sleep before waking.

probable_causes: Waking from a long nap or deep sleep
conditions.isolation_relevance: Crews may be woken for alarms or off-nominal events and must act soon after waking; pilot-error accidents were most common in the first hour after waking, and the most significant inertia effects occur within 30 minutes (Hilditch 2019).
conditions.orientative_interpretation: If you woke up recently, your signals may indicate normal post-waking grogginess. It is usually strongest in the first 30 minutes and fades over about an hour. If possible, allow a short buffer before critical tasks, use bright light and, if appropriate, caffeine.

conditions.name: Pattern consistent with asthenia (space neurasthenia)
conditions.summary: A condition described by Russian space medicine involving fatigue, irritability, emotional lability, difficulty concentrating, sleep and appetite problems and sometimes palpitations, developing over long missions.

indicator_rules.note: Composite fatigue index above personal baseline; no validated absolute threshold; baseline-relative design value.
Heart rate above personal baseline may reflect palpitations or autonomic instability (MedlinePlus Stress); no validated absolute threshold; baseline-relative design value.
RMSSD more than 15% below baseline; stress is associated with reduced parasympathetic (vagal) HRV (Kim 2018 meta-analysis); no validated absolute threshold; baseline-relative design value.
Composite wellbeing index more than 15% below baseline; no validated absolute threshold; baseline-relative design value.
Tiredness and quick loss of strength are core asthenia features (HRP evidence report).
Irritability and unstable mood (HRP evidence report; Kanas 2016).
Difficulty with attention and concentration (local CNS file).
Sleep disturbance (HRP evidence report).
Appetite problems (local CNS file; Kanas 2016).
Cosmonaut data suggest asthenia is unlikely in flights shorter than 4 months (HRP evidence report).
Low or labile mood.
Physical complaints.
Increased sensitivity and nervousness (low sensation threshold).

probable_causes: Cumulative stress of a long mission
Medical causes to rule out (anemia, thyroid, infection)
conditions.isolation_relevance: Russian medical personnel regard asthenia (neurasthenia) as one of the largest threats to cosmonauts' emotional well-being, although NASA flight surgeons have not seen the full cluster in any astronaut and the concept is not recognized in the DSM (HRP evidence report). Increased family contact and surprise supplies have been used as countermeasures (Kanas 2016).
conditions.orientative_interpretation: Your answers suggest a combination of fatigue, irritability, poor concentration and sleep or appetite changes, and your signals may show more strain than your baseline. This combination may indicate the pattern described as asthenia in long missions. It is worth discussing with your flight surgeon, who can also check for physical causes.
conditions.escalation_criteria: If the safety item is answered yes at any time, the app's safety protocol takes priority over this orientation. Refer to the flight surgeon if the fatigue cluster persists for 2 weeks or more, worsens, or comes with palpitations, weight change or low mood, so that medical causes can be checked and the behavioral health team involved.
conditions.camera_limits: Asthenia is a cluster of reported experiences; fatigue and heart-rate signals on camera are non-specific and also reflect sleep loss, deconditioning, anemia or illness.

conditions.name: Pattern consistent with headward fluid shift effects (head fullness, nasal congestion)
conditions.summary: In weightlessness roughly 2 L of fluid moves toward the head within the first hours, producing facial puffiness, sinonasal congestion and headache that can disturb sleep and concentration and be mistaken for low mood or fatigue.

indicator_rules.note: Nasal congestion reported by 75% of ISS astronauts; fluid shift is the main driver (Ax 2025; Khan/TAMU 2025)
Congestion plus cabin CO2 may contribute to frequent in-flight headaches (Ax 2025; OCHMO-TB-004)
Sinonasal symptoms disrupt sleep (Khan/TAMU 2025)
Fatigue reported with sinonasal issues (Khan/TAMU 2025)
Impaired decision-making and productivity when unaddressed (Khan/TAMU 2025)
Non-specific fatigue signal; no validated absolute threshold
Shift occurs within the first 6-10 h of microgravity, symptoms most noticeable early (Ax 2025)

probable_causes: Headward redistribution of blood and cerebrospinal fluid in microgravity
Possible additive vasodilating effect of elevated cabin CO2
Pressure changes between station and suit during EVA preparation (Eustachian tube dysfunction)
conditions.isolation_relevance: Fluid shift is present for the whole time in weightlessness, so congestion, head fullness and the poor sleep it causes can persist for months and lower mood, patience and concentration in a confined crew that cannot simply step outside.
conditions.orientative_interpretation: Your answers may indicate head fullness or nasal congestion that is common in weightlessness. This physical pattern can make you feel tired, irritable or foggy, so it is worth separating it from emotional strain before drawing conclusions about mood. Consider discussing it with your flight surgeon if it disturbs your sleep.
conditions.escalation_criteria: Involve the flight surgeon if congestion or headache persists for more than a few days, disturbs sleep on most nights, needs repeated decongestant use, or comes with any change in vision.
red_flags: New blurred near or distance vision or visual spots
Facial pain with fever (possible sinus infection)
Ear pain or hearing change after pressure changes
conditions.camera_limits: The camera cannot see facial puffiness reliably, cannot measure nasal airflow, intracranial pressure or fluid volumes; heart rate, HRV and expression features are not specific to fluid shift. This pattern rests mainly on self-report.

conditions.name: Pattern consistent with effects of elevated cabin CO2
conditions.summary: Cabin CO2 above about 3 mmHg has been associated with headache, fatigue, poor sleep and reduced concentration in spaceflight; these can look like stress or low mood.

indicator_rules.note: Headaches reported at 2.8-4.5 mmHg ppCO2, worsening with higher CO2 (OCHMO-TB-004)
CO2-related performance concerns; expert opinion, no validated questionnaire cut-off
Fatigue and malaise reported above 4.5 mmHg (OCHMO-TB-004)
Poor sleep reported around 3.5 mmHg; hypercapnia listed among sleep disruptors (OCHMO-TB-004; local CNS file)
CO2 is a vasodilator that may add to nasal engorgement (Ax 2025)
Non-specific; no validated absolute threshold
Drowsiness sign; non-specific; baseline-relative because no CO2-specific threshold exists
KSS 6+ = some signs of sleepiness; non-specific

probable_causes: Cabin ppCO2 above the 3 mmHg one-hour limit (NASA-STD-3001 V2 6004)
Local CO2 pockets from poor airflow (for example in sleep stations or near scrubber-distant nodes)
Individual sensitivity, worsened by fluid shift
conditions.isolation_relevance: In a sealed habitat the crew breathes the same recycled air for months; CO2 can rise with equipment issues and is invisible, so headache and fatigue that several crew share may have an environmental rather than a psychological cause.
conditions.orientative_interpretation: Your answers may indicate headache and tiredness of the kind that has been linked to elevated cabin CO2. This is an environmental check, not a judgement about your mental state. It may help to look at the cabin CO2 reading and airflow before interpreting the rest of this session.
conditions.escalation_criteria: Report to the flight surgeon and ground if several crew members report headache at the same time, if ppCO2 telemetry stays above 3 mmHg, or if headache persists after moving to a well-ventilated area.
red_flags: Several crew with simultaneous headache or confusion
Shortness of breath or rapid breathing at rest
conditions.camera_limits: The camera cannot measure CO2. Facial and cardiac indicators cannot separate CO2 effects from fatigue, stress or fluid shift; this pattern must be confirmed with ECLSS ppCO2 telemetry.

conditions.name: Pattern consistent with possible low iron status (worth a lab check)
conditions.summary: Low iron can cause weakness, fatigue, reduced energy and trouble focusing or remembering, which overlap with depression and sleep loss. Only a blood test can confirm it.

Trouble focusing or remembering (NIH ODS iron; local anemia table)

conditions.isolation_relevance: Fatigue and poor focus on a long mission are easily attributed to stress or monotony. Note that in spaceflight iron stores tend to rise rather than fall (serum ferritin increased 34% after ISS flights), so deficiency is less likely in flight and self-supplementing is not advised.
conditions.orientative_interpretation: Your answers describe low energy and difficulty concentrating that can have many causes, including nutritional ones such as low iron. The camera cannot assess this. It may be worth asking your flight surgeon whether a lab panel is appropriate before assuming the cause is psychological.
conditions.escalation_criteria: Request a lab panel with the flight surgeon if low energy and poor concentration persist for two weeks or more despite adequate sleep. Do not start iron supplements without medical guidance.
red_flags: Shortness of breath or chest discomfort on light exertion

conditions.name: Pattern consistent with medication or stimulant side effects
conditions.summary: Sleep aids, antihistamines, anti-motion-sickness drugs and wake-promoting stimulants are widely used in spaceflight and can cause next-day drowsiness, slowed reactions, nervousness, sleep trouble or mood change.

Drowsiness: promethazine, diphenhydramine, zolpidem next-day effects (MedlinePlus)

Nervousness/restlessness (promethazine); anxiety (modafinil, zolpidem)

countermeasures.title: Slow paced breathing (about 6 breaths per minute)
steps: Sit or float in a stable position and relax your shoulders.
Breathe in gently through your nose for about 4 seconds.
Breathe out slowly for about 6 seconds, so each full breath takes about 10 seconds (about 6 breaths per minute).
Use the on-screen pacer if available and keep the breath light, not forced.
Continue for 5 to 10 minutes, then notice how your body feels.
countermeasures.duration: 5-10 min, once or twice daily or when stressed

sources.title: Lehrer PM, Gevirtz R. Heart rate variability biofeedback: how and why does it work? Front Psychol 2014;5:756
Laborde S, Allen M, Borges U, et al. Effects of voluntary slow breathing on heart rate and heart rate variability: a systematic review and a meta-analysis. Neurosci Biobehav Rev 2022
NCCIH Clinical Digest: Mind and Body Approaches for Stress and Anxiety: What the Science Says

countermeasures.notes: Resonance frequency for most adults is about 6 breaths per minute (0.1 Hz) (Lehrer & Gevirtz 2014). A meta-analysis of 223 studies found voluntary slow breathing increases vagally mediated HRV (Laborde 2022). The 4 s / 6 s split is one practical way to reach about 10 s per breath; stop if lightheaded.

countermeasures.title: Box breathing (4-4-4-4)
steps: Breathe out slowly to empty your lungs.
Breathe in through your nose while counting slowly to four.
Hold your breath for a count of four.
Breathe out for a count of four, then hold for a count of four.
Repeat for three to four rounds.
countermeasures.duration: 3-4 rounds (about 1-2 min), one or two sessions a day

sources.title: Cleveland Clinic: Box Breathing
Balban MY, Neri E, Kogon MM, et al. Brief structured respiration practices enhance mood and reduce physiological arousal. Cell Rep Med 2023 (doi:10.1016/j.xcrm.2022.100895)

countermeasures.notes: Box breathing was one of the active arms in Balban et al. 2023; cyclic sighing produced larger mood benefits. Skip breath holds if they cause discomfort.

countermeasures.title: Cyclic sighing (physiological sigh)
steps: Breathe in through your nose until your lungs feel comfortably full.
Take a second, short top-up inhale through the nose.
Breathe out slowly and fully through your mouth, making the exhale longer than the two inhales.
Repeat at a relaxed pace, emphasising the long exhale.
Continue for 5 minutes; once a day is the studied dose.

sources.title: Balban MY, Neri E, Kogon MM, et al. Brief structured respiration practices enhance mood and reduce physiological arousal. Cell Rep Med 2023 (doi:10.1016/j.xcrm.2022.100895)

countermeasures.notes: In a remote randomized controlled trial (about 1 month of daily 5-minute practice), cyclic sighing improved mood and reduced respiratory rate more than mindfulness meditation (Balban 2023).

countermeasures.title: Progressive muscle relaxation
steps: Find a place where you will not be disturbed and secure yourself in position.
Tense one muscle group (for example fists) for about 5 seconds while breathing in; never hold your breath.
Release all at once while breathing out and notice the feeling of relaxation.
Move through the groups: hands, arms, forehead, eyes, jaw, neck, shoulders, stomach, back, legs, feet.
Ease off or skip any muscle that hurts or cramps.

sources.title: VA Whole Health Library: Progressive Muscle Relaxation (Mirgain SA, Singles J)
NCCIH Clinical Digest: Mind and Body Approaches for Stress and Anxiety: What the Science Says

Edinger JD, Arnedt JT, Bertisch SM, et al. Behavioral and psychological treatments for chronic insomnia disorder in adults: an AASM clinical practice guideline. J Clin Sleep Med 2021 (NeurologyLive summary)

countermeasures.notes: Relaxation as a single-component insomnia therapy has a conditional recommendation (AASM, Edinger 2021).

countermeasures.title: Body scan
steps: Close your eyes or lower your gaze and take three slow breaths.
Move attention slowly from the top of your head down to your feet.
Notice tension, warmth or pressure in each area without trying to change it.
When the mind wanders, gently return to the body part you were on.
Finish with two slow breaths and notice the body as a whole.

sources.title: NCCIH Clinical Digest: Mind and Body Approaches for Stress and Anxiety: What the Science Says

countermeasures.notes: Body scan is a common mindfulness practice; the cited evidence covers mindfulness programs in general rather than body scan alone.

countermeasures.title: Brief mindfulness practice
steps: Set a 10-minute timer and settle into a stable position.
Rest attention on the sensation of breathing.
When thoughts arise, label them briefly ('thinking') and return to the breath.
Be patient with wandering; returning attention is the practice.
End by noting one thing you can see and one thing you can hear.

sources.title: NCCIH Clinical Digest: Mind and Body Approaches for Stress and Anxiety: What the Science Says

countermeasures.notes: Mindfulness-based stress reduction was noninferior to escitalopram for anxiety disorders in a 2023 RCT, and a 2014 meta-analysis of 47 trials showed moderate evidence for anxiety and depression (NCCIH 2024). Some people report increased anxiety; stop if distressing.

countermeasures.title: 5-4-3-2-1 grounding
steps: Settle and take one slow, deep breath.
Notice 5 things you can see.
Notice 4 things you can feel.
Notice 3 things you can hear and 2 things you can smell.
Notice 1 thing you can taste, then take another slow breath.

sources.title: NHS inform: Grounding exercises

countermeasures.title: Catch it, check it, change it (reframing unhelpful thoughts)
steps: Catch it: notice the unhelpful thought as it happens (for example expecting the worst).
Write the thought down in a few words.
Check it: look at the evidence for and against it and consider other explanations.
Change it: write a more balanced thought that fits the evidence.
Notice how your feeling changes after the new thought.

sources.title: NHS Every Mind Matters: Reframing unhelpful thoughts
NIMH: I'm So Stressed Out! Fact Sheet
NIMH: Generalized Anxiety Disorder: When Worry Gets Out of Control

countermeasures.notes: Identifying and challenging unhelpful thoughts is a core CBT skill; NIMH describes CBT as the gold-standard psychotherapy for GAD.

countermeasures.title: Scheduled worry window (worry postponement)
steps: Choose one fixed, short period each day for worrying, not close to bedtime.
When a worry appears outside that time, jot a brief note and postpone it.
Separate real, solvable problems from hypothetical 'what ifs'.
During the window, review the notes and plan an action for solvable items.
Over time, notice whether postponed worries feel less urgent.
countermeasures.duration: one short daily period (length not specified by source)

sources.title: Psychology Tools: Worry Postponement (citing Borkovec TD, et al. Stimulus control applications to the treatment of worry. Behav Res Ther 1983;21(3):247-251)

countermeasures.notes: Introduced as a stimulus-control task by Borkovec et al. (1983) and reported to reduce daily worry.

countermeasures.title: Behavioral activation
steps: Keep a simple daily log of activities and rate each for accomplishment and pleasure (0-10).
Identify activities linked to better mood and those you have been avoiding.
Schedule two small, specific activities for the coming week at set times.
Do them according to plan rather than waiting for motivation.
Break larger goals into small graded steps and review progress weekly.

sources.title: Hunnicutt-Ferguson K. Behavioral Activation for Major Depressive Disorder. Emory University School of Medicine
NIMH: Depression (NIH Publication No. 24-MH-8079)

countermeasures.notes: BA is supported by randomized trials as effective for depression, comparable to cognitive therapy and medication at follow-up (Dimidjian 2006; Dobson 2008, as summarized by Emory).

countermeasures.title: Pleasant activity scheduling
steps: List activities you enjoy or used to enjoy that are possible on board (music, films, photography, calls, games).
Choose one or two small ones and put them in your schedule at a fixed time.
Treat them as protected time, like a work task.
Afterwards, rate the enjoyment from 0 to 10.
Keep the ones that help and rotate in new ones.
countermeasures.duration: short, scheduled sessions; start with two per week

sources.title: Hunnicutt-Ferguson K. Behavioral Activation for Major Depressive Disorder. Emory University School of Medicine
Slack KJ, Schneiderman JS, Leveton LB, Whitmire AM, Picano JJ. Evidence Report: Risk of Adverse Cognitive or Behavioral Conditions and Psychiatric Disorders. NASA Human Research Program

countermeasures.title: Three good things journal
steps: At the end of the day, write down three things that went well.
Give each a short title.
Describe what happened and how it made you feel.
Note what you think caused it.
If you drift to negatives, refocus on the good event.
countermeasures.duration: 10 min daily for at least one week

sources.title: Greater Good in Action (UC Berkeley): Three Good Things (citing Seligman MEP, et al. Am Psychol 2005)

countermeasures.notes: Seligman et al. (2005) reported increased happiness that persisted at six months.

countermeasures.title: Expressive writing
steps: Find a private time and space.
Write continuously about a stressful or emotional experience, without worrying about spelling or grammar.
Write for 15-20 minutes per session on up to four consecutive days.
Avoid topics that feel too overwhelming right now.
If you feel very distressed, stop and use a calming activity such as slow breathing or talking with someone.

sources.title: VA Whole Health Library: What Is Therapeutic Journaling? (Mirgain SA, Singles J)
Stuster J. Behavioral Issues Associated With Long Duration Space Expeditions: Review and Analysis of Astronaut Journals (NASA JSC-CN-21128)

countermeasures.notes: Feeling sad after writing is common and usually passes within hours. Astronauts reported that journaling helped them maintain perspective (Stuster 2010).

countermeasures.title: Task chunking and graded steps
steps: Split a large or long task into small, clearly defined steps.
Do the first step only and check it off.
Insert a short break between blocks of demanding work.
Put the hardest steps at your most alert time of day.
Review what is done before moving on.

sources.title: Hunnicutt-Ferguson K. Behavioral Activation for Major Depressive Disorder. Emory University School of Medicine
Lim J, Dinges DF. Sleep deprivation and vigilant attention. Ann N Y Acad Sci 2008;1129:305-322

countermeasures.notes: Graded task assignment is part of behavioral activation; vigilance declines with time on task, especially with sleep loss (Lim & Dinges 2008).

countermeasures.title: Micro-breaks
steps: Pause the current task for a short break of 10 minutes or less.
Change posture or move, look away from screens, or do a short breathing exercise.
Avoid starting another demanding task during the break.
Return to the task and notice energy and focus.
For very demanding cognitive work, plan longer breaks.
countermeasures.duration: 10 min or less, several times per work period

sources.title: Albulescu P, et al. 'Give me a break!' A systematic review and meta-analysis on the efficacy of micro-breaks for increasing well-being and performance. PLoS ONE 2022;17(8):e0272460

countermeasures.notes: A meta-analysis of 22 studies found micro-breaks associated with higher vigor and lower fatigue, but not with better performance overall; longer breaks may be needed for performance (Albulescu 2022).

countermeasures.title: Cognitive workload review
steps: List upcoming tasks and mark which are high cognitive demand.
Identify periods where several demanding tasks overlap.
Discuss sequencing or support options with the crew and ground team.
Plan breaks and handovers for long monitoring tasks.
Re-check after changes and repeat if workload stays high.
countermeasures.duration: short planning review, repeat as needed

countermeasures.title: Private family conference
steps: Request or confirm your next private family conference slot.
Prepare a few things you would like to share or ask.
Use a private space during the call.
If real-time contact is not possible, record a message or write a letter.
Afterwards, take a few minutes for yourself before returning to work.

countermeasures.title: Shared crew meal or social time
steps: Agree a regular time for a shared meal or social break.
Keep it light: no work topics for part of the time.
Rotate who chooses the menu, music or theme.
Use it to celebrate small milestones or personal events.
Respect people who need to skip occasionally.
countermeasures.duration: regular, at a frequency agreed by the crew

countermeasures.title: Protected private time
steps: Agree with the crew on a regular block of private, undisturbed time.
Use your private quarters or a quiet area and signal 'do not disturb'.
Choose a restorative activity (music, reading, writing, calling home).
Keep work communications off during this time when operations allow.
countermeasures.duration: regular blocks agreed by the crew

countermeasures.title: Calm conflict debrief
steps: Wait until both people feel calm, then agree a private time to talk.
Each person describes the situation from their own view without interruption.
Focus on the specific issue and its effect on work, not on personalities.
Agree on one concrete change each person will try.
If it stays unresolved or affects safety, involve the commander or behavioral health team.
countermeasures.duration: one short private conversation, repeat if needed

countermeasures.title: Peer support check-in
steps: Choose a trusted crewmate or contact on Earth.
Share briefly how you are doing, including what is hard.
Listen in return and ask how they are doing.
Agree a simple follow-up (for example a check-in in a few days).
Humor and shared activities can help reduce tension.

countermeasures.title: Behavioral health consultation
steps: Request a private psychological conference with the behavioral health team or flight surgeon.
Share the ASTRAVITA summary and your questionnaire answers if you wish.
Describe how long symptoms have lasted and how they affect work and sleep.
Agree on a follow-up plan and any monitoring.
If you have thoughts of harming yourself, follow the safety protocol immediately.
countermeasures.duration: per schedule; urgent if safety concern

countermeasures.title: Sleep environment and habits check
steps: Keep the sleep area quiet, cool and dark; use earplugs, eye mask or light blockers if needed.
Avoid caffeine and nicotine later in the day.
Avoid bright screens and intense exercise in the hour before sleep.
Keep naps to 20 minutes or less if you have trouble sleeping at night.
Keep a consistent sleep and wake schedule.

countermeasures.notes: Sleep hygiene alone is not recommended as a stand-alone insomnia treatment (AASM 2021), but it supports multi-component approaches.

countermeasures.title: Anchor your sleep schedule
steps: Set a fixed wake-up time and keep it every day.
Keep sleep and wake times within about an hour of each other across days.
Plan your sleep period backwards from the fixed wake time.
Get light and activity soon after waking to reinforce the schedule.

sources.title: NHLBI: Sleep Deprivation and Deficiency - Healthy Sleep Habits
Stanford Health Care: Stimulus Control and CBTI
NIMH: Depression (NIH Publication No. 24-MH-8079)

countermeasures.title: Strategic short nap
steps: Plan the nap ahead of critical tasks, ideally earlier in the work period.
Keep it short: about 20-30 minutes of sleep.
Set an alarm and allow time to recover from grogginess before critical work.
Avoid long naps if you have trouble sleeping at night.
If allowed, caffeine taken just before a short nap may reduce post-nap grogginess.

countermeasures.notes: NASA pilots given a 40-minute nap opportunity (about 26 minutes of sleep) showed up to 54% higher alertness and 34% better performance (Rosekind 1995). NHLBI advises naps of 20 minutes or less; naps of 30 minutes or less reduce sleep inertia (Hilditch 2019).

countermeasures.title: Caffeine timing
steps: Use caffeine strategically for alertness early in the work period.
Stop caffeine at least 6 hours before your planned sleep; effects can last up to 8 hours.
Avoid stacking doses when already anxious or jittery.
Record caffeine intake if sleep is poor, and share it with the flight surgeon.

sources.title: Drake C, et al. Caffeine effects on sleep taken 0, 3, or 6 hours before going to bed. J Clin Sleep Med 2013 (AASM release)

countermeasures.title: Pre-sleep wind-down routine
steps: Switch habitat lighting to the pre-sleep (dim, low-blue) setting.
Stop work tasks and bright screens before sleep.
Do a calming activity: slow breathing, muscle relaxation or light reading.
Avoid intense exercise in the last hour before sleep.
Go to your sleep station at the same time each night.

countermeasures.title: Stimulus control (CBT-I component)
steps: Keep a regular morning rise time every day.
Go to bed only when sleepy, not just tired.
Use the sleep station only for sleep.
If you cannot fall asleep or fall back asleep, get up and do something calm in dim light; return only when sleepy.
Avoid long naps; a brief 15-30 minute nap is acceptable.
countermeasures.duration: nightly, as part of a clinician-guided plan

countermeasures.notes: Multi-component CBT-I has a strong recommendation; stimulus control alone has a conditional recommendation (AASM, Edinger 2021). A full CBT-I course should be guided by a clinician.

countermeasures.title: Bright light at the start of the day
steps: Switch habitat lighting to the bright, blue-enriched setting at the start of your day.
If a light box is available, use about 10,000 lux for at least 30 minutes in the morning.
Keep your eyes open and face the light source without staring directly into it.
Check with the flight surgeon first if you have eye conditions or take light-sensitizing medication.

Reduce screen brightness or use night mode on displays.

Use light blockers or an eye mask in the sleep station.

steps: Before a schedule shift, agree a lighting plan with the flight surgeon or mission planning.

Use the dim pre-sleep setting and block light before the new sleep period.
Shift sleep and meals together with the light schedule.

Discuss priorities with the commander and ground team.
Protect sleep and off-duty periods in the revised plan.
Review again after one week.

countermeasures.title: Crew self-scheduling
steps: Identify tasks whose timing can be chosen by the crew.

countermeasures.title: Add novelty and variety
steps: Change something small in your routine (order of tasks, exercise program, music).
Open a care package or new media saved for later in the mission.
Start a short new project or learning goal.
Rearrange or personalize part of your personal space.

countermeasures.title: Leisure and hobby time
steps: Choose a hobby available on board (music, reading, photography, games, drawing).
Schedule it as protected time.
Combine with exercise when possible (for example music or films during workouts).
Share hobbies with crewmates occasionally.

steps: Choose a nature scene you personally prefer (forest, beach, countryside).
Use a VR headset or large display in a quiet spot.
Watch for about 15 minutes while breathing slowly.
Notice how your body feels afterwards and rate your mood.

steps: Break the remaining mission into shorter segments (for example by month or quarter).
Plan a small celebration or ritual at each milestone (halfway point, arrivals, holidays).
Keep a visible countdown or progress record.
Look ahead to concrete post-mission plans with family.

countermeasures.title: Moderate aerobic exercise session
steps: Use the treadmill or cycle ergometer (T2 / CEVIS) within your scheduled exercise block.
Warm up for 5 minutes at an easy pace.
Exercise for 20-30 minutes at a moderate effort where you can talk but not sing.
Cool down for 5 minutes and drink water afterwards.
Aim across the week for at least 150-300 minutes of moderate to vigorous aerobic activity, counting your prescribed countermeasure exercise.

countermeasures.title: Resistance training session
steps: Use the resistive device (ARED or equivalent) following your prescribed protocol.
Do 2-3 sets of 8-12 repetitions for major muscle groups (legs, back, chest, shoulders).
Move with control and breathe out during the effort phase; do not hold your breath.
Rest 1-2 minutes between sets.
Note mood and energy before and after to see your own response.

countermeasures.title: Posture and stretching break
steps: Stop the current task and move away from the workstation if possible.
Slowly roll the shoulders backwards 5 times.
Gently turn the head left and right and tilt each ear toward the shoulder, holding each stretch 15-20 seconds without pain.
Stretch the upper back by reaching both arms forward and rounding the back.
Before resuming, check screen distance and posture (back supported, screen slightly below eye level).

countermeasures.title: Neck and shoulder tension release
steps: Sit or anchor comfortably and let the shoulders drop away from the ears.
Massage the base of the skull, temples and upper shoulders with your fingertips for 1-2 minutes.
Apply a warm (or cold, if preferred) pack to the neck or shoulders for up to 10 minutes.
Finish with slow neck stretches, holding each 15-20 seconds.
Note any trigger (posture, long fixed task, cold air) in a headache diary.

countermeasures.title: Jaw relaxation
steps: Notice whether your teeth are clenched; let the lips close lightly with the teeth slightly apart and the tongue resting.
Place warm or cool packs on the jaw muscles for a few minutes.
Gently open and close the mouth slowly 5-10 times within a pain-free range.
Reduce gum chewing and nail biting during the day.
Combine with a short relaxation or breathing exercise if stress is high.

countermeasures.title: Hydration check
steps: Ask yourself: am I thirsty, is my mouth dry, has my urine been darker or less frequent today?
Drink a glass of water now and keep a personal drink bag or bottle within reach.
Drink more around exercise, heat, illness or vomiting.
Re-check headache and alertness after 30-60 minutes.
Before gravity re-exposure, follow the flight surgeon's fluid and salt loading protocol.

countermeasures.title: Review iron intake with the nutrition team
steps: Note which iron-containing foods you actually eat (meat, seafood, poultry, fortified cereals, beans, lentils, spinach).
Pair plant-based iron foods with a vitamin C source (citrus, tomatoes, broccoli) to improve absorption.
Do not start iron supplements on your own; in spaceflight iron stores tend to rise and excess iron can be harmful.
Discuss intake and any lab results with the flight surgeon or mission nutritionist.

steps: Check whether your menu regularly includes B12 sources (animal-derived or fortified foods), especially if you eat a mostly plant-based diet.

Report numbness, tingling or balance problems to the flight surgeon.
Ask whether a serum B12 test (with methylmalonic acid confirmation if low) is appropriate; avoid high-dose supplements without guidance.

countermeasures.title: Review vitamin D supplementation
steps: Confirm you are taking the vitamin D supplement prescribed for the mission; there is no UVB exposure in the habitat.
The adult RDA is 600 IU (15 mcg) per day up to age 70; do not exceed 4,000 IU (100 mcg) per day without medical advice.
Ask the flight surgeon whether a 25(OH)D blood level is due, especially in the second half of the mission.
Remember that vitamin D is not a treatment for low mood on its own; keep other supports in place.

countermeasures.title: Regular, unhurried meals
steps: Schedule meals at consistent times and protect them from task overrun.
Eat the planned menu items even if appetite is reduced; choose lighter meals if you feel lightheaded after heavy meals.
Drink water with each meal.
Tell the flight surgeon or nutritionist about persistent appetite change or unintended weight change.

Watch for side effects such as headache, fast or pounding heartbeat, anxiety or mood change.

Agree on follow-up checks and when to call earlier.

steps: List all medications, sleep aids and anti-motion-sickness drugs taken in the last 72 hours with times and doses.

steps: Read a standard near-vision card or familiar text at your usual distance and note any new blur.

countermeasures.title: Blood pressure and orthostatic check
steps: Measure blood pressure and pulse after 5 minutes of quiet rest (typical adult resting values: BP 90/60-120/80 mmHg, pulse 60-100 bpm).
In a gravity environment, stand up slowly and repeat the measurement at 1 and 3 minutes.
A drop of more than 20 mmHg systolic or 10 mmHg diastolic within 3 minutes of standing suggests orthostatic hypotension.
Sit down immediately if lightheaded, and share the readings with the flight surgeon.

countermeasures.title: Cabin CO2 and ventilation check
steps: Check the current and recent cabin ppCO2 readings (limit: 3 mmHg one-hour average, NASA-STD-3001 V2 6004).
Check whether other crew members have similar headaches.
Make sure your sleep station and work area fans are on and unobstructed; adjust airflow so you are not in a stagnant pocket.
Move to a better-ventilated module for a while if symptoms persist.
Report sustained high readings or scrubber issues to the ground and the flight surgeon.

countermeasures.title: Head-elevated rest (gravity environments only)
steps: Applies on a planetary surface, in analog habitats or after landing, not in weightlessness.
Raise the head of the bed or use extra pillows when resting or sleeping.
Give yourself extra time when getting up: sit first, then stand while holding something sturdy.
Avoid very hot showers and heavy meals when you feel lightheaded.
In weightlessness, discuss mechanical countermeasures (for example thigh cuffs) with the flight surgeon instead.

countermeasures.title: Veno-constrictive thigh cuffs (Braslet-type), only under flight surgeon guidance
steps: Use only if prescribed by the flight surgeon and following the fitting procedure.
Ground studies wore cuffs about 10 hours per day at a pressure of about 30 mmHg and removed them overnight.
Watch for numbness, pain, color change or swelling of the legs and remove the cuffs if they occur.
Do not wear them continuously for 24 hours (venous thrombosis concern).
Note any relief of head fullness or congestion for your medical conference.

countermeasures.title: Noise check and reduction
steps: Identify the main noise source in your work or sleep area (fans, pumps, intermittent hardware).
Report unusually loud or new noises; regular maintenance and isolating vibrating equipment reduce off-nominal noise.
Close your crew quarters and use approved sound-dampening measures where available.
Use personal hearing protection for sleep only if your crew procedures allow it (it must not replace engineering noise limits or block alarms).
Keep personal audio at moderate volume.

countermeasures.title: Thermal comfort adjustment
steps: Check cabin temperature and humidity (comfort zone 20-25 C and 30-60% relative humidity, NASA-STD-3001 V2 6013).
Adjust your sleep station airflow and clothing layers.
Add a layer if you are cold, especially at night; cold can trigger tension headaches.
Report sustained readings outside the comfort zone to the crew and ground.

countermeasures.title: 20-20-20 eye rest and screen setup
steps: Every 20 minutes, take a 20-second break and look at something about 20 feet (6 m) away.
Blink fully and deliberately several times during each break.
Keep the screen about 20-28 inches (50-70 cm) from your eyes and 15-20 degrees below eye level.
Reduce glare on the screen.
If blurring persists after breaks, request a vision check.

hr_bpm.population: Healthy adults at rest (sitting or lying, calm)
hr_bpm.notes: AHA and MedlinePlus normal adult resting range. Fit individuals often rest below 60. Emotions, pain, temperature, medications and standing up change HR. Use baseline-relative rules for interpretation; rPPG estimates have extra error.

rmssd_ms.population: Healthy adults, short-term (about 5 min) resting recordings; 44 studies, 21,438 participants
rmssd_ms.notes: Nunan et al. 2010 short-term norm: mean 42 (SD 15) ms, range 19-75 ms (15 studies), reproduced in Shaffer & Ginsberg 2017 Table 6. RMSSD is the primary time-domain index of vagally mediated HRV. Conventional minimum recording is 5 min; ultra-short (10-60 s) measures are not standardized. Large inter-individual variation and decline with age: use personal baseline, not population limits, for decisions.

sources.title: MedlinePlus: Vital signs

blink_rate_min.notes: Normal spontaneous blink rate 12-15/min (Doughty 2001) and up to 22/min mean in relaxed conditions (Tsubota & Nakamori 1993), both as cited in Abusharha 2017; that study's own relaxed baseline was 19.7 +/- 9.1/min. Screen and reading tasks reduce blinking: by 56% in normal subjects during a demanding computer task (Himebaugh 2009); 17/min in conversation to 6/min reading on a screen in dry-eye patients (Schlote 2004). Very large individual variation: use baseline-relative rules. Blink duration is about 100-400 ms (Soukupova & Cech 2016). Blink frequency is listed as a drowsiness indicator in the local files but none gives a validated cut-off.

perclos_pct.unit: % of time eyes at least 80% closed (P80)
perclos_pct.notes: Definition (P80): proportion of time in a minute that the eyes are at least 80% closed (Wierwille et al. 1994, FHWA/FMCSA tech brief FHWA-MCRT-98-006, 1998, Dinges et al.). Closed is usually defined as eyelid less than 20% open; some studies use less than 25% or 30% open. Fast blinks (under 250 ms, Dinges 1998; or under 400-500 ms) are excluded. Eye closure longer than 500 ms is treated as a behavioral microsleep. Abe 2023 review: definitions vary widely and there is no single accepted drowsiness cut-off. Example cut-offs in use: NHTSA/VTTI 2009 drowsy-driver warning study analysed episodes with manual PERCLOS above 12 (units presumed %, not confirmed in the excerpt read); local file applsci-15-00638 (2025) set a PERCLOS threshold of 0.2 (20%) over 3-s windows at 30 fps; local file sensors-24-07810 (2024) describes PERCLOS as percentage of time per minute that eyes are at least 80% closed. The 'high' value of 12 is a literature example, not a validated universal limit; prefer baseline-relative rules.

ear_closed_threshold.population: Adults in webcam/driver datasets (68-point dlib landmarks)
ear_closed_threshold.notes: EAR = (|p2-p6| + |p3-p5|) / (2|p1-p4|). Soukupova & Cech 2016 use a baseline threshold of 0.2 (not derived; noted to fail with smiling, side views and long closures); measured open-eye EAR about 0.4 +/- 0.1 and closed about 0.05 +/- 0.05. Local thesis 20250804162141-2782-TL (BUAP 2025) uses 0.25 (taken from Thi Hien et al.) and notes a fully closed eye falls below 0.1; its implementation averages EAR over 30 consecutive frames and multiplies the user's thresholds by calibration factors before raising an eye-closure alert. sensors-24-07810 uses the same EAR formula (reports 94.9% accuracy for EAR-only methods in a separate study). Recommendation: calibrate per user (for example a fraction of the person's open-eye EAR) rather than a fixed value.

mar_yawn_threshold.notes: Local thesis 20250804162141-2782-TL (2025), following Thi Hien et al., computes MAR = (|p2-p12| + |p3-p11| + |p4-p10| + |p5-p9| + |p6-p8|) / (5|p1-p7|) on outer-lip points and classifies any MAR above 0.7 as a yawn. The value depends on the exact MAR formula and landmark set, so it must be re-checked if a different formula is used. applsci-15-00638 (2025) uses a different metric (POM, percentage of mouth opening over time) with a threshold of 0.5 in 3-s windows; 2025.naacl-demo.7 compares lip-to-center distance ratios with an unspecified threshold.

head_pose.notes: 2025.naacl-demo.7 (Xie & Fan, NAACL 2025 demo) recommends judging head nodding/inclination with Pitch <= -16 deg or >= 16 deg and Roll <= -35 deg or >= 35 deg, noting angles may deviate and can be tuned; it flags inattentiveness at Yaw +/-60 deg, Pitch +/-30 deg, Roll +/-30 deg, and raises an alert when more than five frames in the buffer indicate fatigue. applsci-15-00638 (2025) estimates yaw, pitch and roll with HOPEnet and classifies head state (still, looking aside, nodding) with machine learning but gives no numeric angle threshold. These are driver-monitoring values; in microgravity posture differs, so use the person's own baseline for head_stability_pct.

questionnaire.title: ASTRAVITA wellbeing check-in
questionnaire.recall_period: Over the last 2 weeks, unless the question says otherwise (sleepiness: right now; sleep hours: last 24 hours; medication: last 72 hours).
questionnaire.instructions: There are no right or wrong answers. Your answers help the app give a more accurate orientation; they are not a diagnosis.

items.text: Over the last 2 weeks, how often have you been bothered by feeling down, depressed, or hopeless?
items.note: PHQ-2 item 2 (public domain wording). PHQ-2 total = q_anhedonia + q_mood_low (0-6); total >= 3 suggests follow-up with PHQ-9.

items.text: Over the last 2 weeks, how often have you been bothered by little interest or pleasure in doing things?
items.note: PHQ-2 item 1 (public domain wording).

items.text: Over the last 2 weeks, how often have you been bothered by feeling nervous, anxious or on edge?
items.note: GAD-2 item 1. GAD-2 total = q_nervous + q_worry (0-6); total >= 3 suggests further evaluation.

items.text: Over the last 2 weeks, how often have you been bothered by not being able to stop or control worrying?
items.note: GAD-2 item 2.

items.text: Over the last 2 weeks, how would you rate your overall sleep quality?
items.note: Single global item informed by the Insomnia Severity Index (sleep satisfaction); not a validated stand-alone scale.

items.text: About how many hours did you actually sleep in the last 24 hours (including naps)?
items.note: Adults need at least 7 hours per day (CDC); in-flight averages were about 6 h (Barger 2014).

items.text: How sleepy do you feel right now?

options.label: Sleepy, but no effort to keep awake
Sleepy, some effort to keep awake
Very sleepy, great effort to keep awake, fighting sleep

items.note: Karolinska Sleepiness Scale 1-9 (Akerstedt & Gillberg 1990); anchors follow the commonly used 9-label version.

items.text: Over the last 2 weeks, how often have you felt isolated from others or lacking companionship?
items.note: Adapted from the 3-item UCLA loneliness scale (Hughes 2004), which uses three options (hardly ever / some of the time / often) per item; a fourth option was added to match the app's 0-3 scale.

items.text: Over the last 2 weeks, how often has your workload felt like more than you could manage?
items.note: Project item; 3 = overwhelming nearly every day.

items.text: Over the last 2 weeks, how often have you felt irritable, short-tempered or easily upset?
items.note: Project item based on symptom lists from NIMH and MedlinePlus.

items.text: Over the last 2 weeks, how often have you had tension or disagreements with crewmates or the ground team?
items.note: Project item.

items.text: Over the last 2 weeks, how often have you been bothered by headaches or muscle aches?
items.note: Project item.

items.text: Over the last 2 weeks, how often have you noticed facial puffiness or a stuffy nose?
items.note: Project item; used mainly by physiological conditions (agent B). Nasal congestion is a reported in-flight complaint (local CNS file).

items.text: Over the last 2 weeks, how often have you been bothered by feeling tired or having little energy?
items.note: Adapted from a PHQ-9 item.

items.text: Over the last 2 weeks, how often have you felt unusually cold when others were comfortable?
items.note: Project item; used mainly by endocrine/nutritional conditions (agent B).

items.text: Over the last 2 weeks, how often have you been bothered by poor appetite or overeating?
items.note: Adapted from a PHQ-9 item.

items.text: Over the last 2 weeks, how often have you had trouble concentrating on things, such as reading or monitoring tasks?
items.note: Adapted from a PHQ-9 item.

items.text: In the last 72 hours, have you started or changed any medication, sleep aid or stimulant?
items.note: Medication can alter sleep, heart rate and alertness; about 75% of ISS crew reported using sleep medication at some point (Barger 2014).

items.text: Over the last 2 weeks, how often have you been bothered by missing home or worrying about family on Earth?
items.note: Project item.

items.text: Over the last 2 weeks, how often have you felt bored or that every day is the same?
items.note: Project item.

items.text: Which part of the mission are you in now?
items.note: Used for adjustment and third-quarter patterns; can be filled automatically from the mission timeline.

safety_item.text: Over the last 2 weeks, have you had thoughts that you would be better off dead, or of hurting yourself in some way?
safety_item.note: Wording adapted from PHQ-9 item 9 to a yes/no format. Any 'yes' triggers the app safety protocol (immediate contact with the flight surgeon / behavioral health team; on Earth, local emergency services or a crisis line such as 988 in the US). Never used in condition scoring.

scoring_notes: PHQ-2 total = q_anhedonia + q_mood_low (0-6); >= 3 is the validated screening cut-point (Kroenke 2003).
GAD-2 total = q_nervous + q_worry (0-6); >= 3 is the preferred cut-point (Kroenke 2007).
A positive PHQ-2 or GAD-2 is not a diagnosis; follow with PHQ-9 / GAD-7 or a clinician interview (PHQ-9 >= 10 and GAD-7 >= 10 are the moderate thresholds; Kroenke 2001, Spitzer 2006).
KSS (1-9): higher = sleepier; scores rise with time awake and vary with time of day.
